# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like: a room full of people who started out with different views and ended up aligned. Someone summarizes the decision, heads nod, and everyone walks out feeling that progress was made. Managers often chase this feeling. Consensus, we assume, is the sign that a group has done its thinking well.

But this picture deserves scrutiny. Agreement is not always evidence that a problem has been solved. Sometimes it is evidence that a problem has been papered over. People nod for many reasons besides conviction: they are tired, they don't want to be the difficult one, they sense the boss has already decided, or they simply haven't had time to form a real opinion. When a meeting ends in easy agreement, the honest conclusion is often not "we have resolved this" but "we have stopped talking about this." The disagreement hasn't disappeared; it has just been moved out of the room, where it will resurface later—usually at a worse and more expensive moment.
